Let $T=(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^r$, where $r\ge0$ is an integer, be a compact torus and $M$ a compact smooth manifold without boundary. A smooth left $T$-action is a jointly smooth map $a:T\times M\to M$ with $a(e,x)=x$ and $a(st,x)=a(s,a(t,x))$. Let $E^0,\ldots,E^N$ be finite-rank complex vector bundles on $M$. For each $j<N$, let $d_j:C^\infty(M,E^j)\to C^\infty(M,E^{j+1})$ be a linear differential operator of finite order $m_j$, and put $d_{-1}=d_N=0$. In local coordinates and bundle frames, if $d_j=\sum_{|\alpha|\le m_j}a_{j,\alpha}(x)\partial_x^\alpha$, use the positive-frequency principal symbol $\sigma(d_j)(x,\xi)=\sum_{|\alpha|=m_j}a_{j,\alpha}(x)(i\xi)^\alpha$. The sequence is a complex when $d_{j+1}d_j=0$ for every $j$. It is **elliptic** when, for every $x\in M$ and every nonzero real cotangent vector $\xi\in T_x^*M$, the sequence of principal-symbol maps

$$0\longrightarrow E_x^0\xrightarrow{\sigma(d_0)(x,\xi)}E_x^1\xrightarrow{\sigma(d_1)(x,\xi)}\cdots\xrightarrow{\sigma(d_{N-1})(x,\xi)}E_x^N\longrightarrow0$$

is exact. Suppose each bundle has a $T$-linearization: a jointly smooth map $T\times E^j\to E^j$ whose restrictions $\rho_t^j(x):E_x^j\to E_{t\cdot x}^j$ are complex-linear isomorphisms, with $\rho_e^j(x)=I_{E_x^j}$ and $\rho_{st}^j(x)=\rho_s^j(t\cdot x)\circ\rho_t^j(x)$. The induced section maps

$$ (U_t^j s)(x):=\rho_t^j(t^{-1}\cdot x)\bigl(s(t^{-1}\cdot x)\bigr) $$

commute with $d_j$. Require the cohomology spaces $H^j(E^\bullet):=\ker d_j/\operatorname{im}d_{j-1}$ to be finite-dimensional. The representation ring $R(T)$ is the Grothendieck ring of finite-dimensional continuous complex representations of $T$. Define

$$\operatorname{Ind}_T(E^\bullet):=\sum_{j=0}^N(-1)^j[H^j(E^\bullet)]\in R(T),\qquad \chi_{E^\bullet}(t):=\sum_{j=0}^N(-1)^j\operatorname{tr}\!\left(U_t^j\bigm|_{H^j(E^\bullet)}\right).$$

For a two-term complex $0\to C^\infty(M,E^+)\xrightarrow{D^+}C^\infty(M,E^-)\to0$, this gives $[\ker D^+]-[\operatorname{coker}D^+]$. This definition concerns elliptic complexes, not transversally elliptic operators.

Assume countable choice. Let $M$ be a compact smooth Riemannian manifold without boundary, $n=\dim M>0$, and $E$ a finite-rank Hermitian bundle. Let $P:C^\infty(M,E)\to C^\infty(M,E)$ be a smooth second-order differential operator. In local coordinates and a bundle frame, write $P=\sum_{|\alpha|\le2}a_\alpha(x)\partial_x^\alpha$ and define its positive-frequency principal symbol by $p(x,\xi)=\sum_{|\alpha|=2}a_\alpha(x)(i\xi)^\alpha$ (equivalently, the coefficient of $\lambda^2$ in $e^{-i\lambda f}P(e^{i\lambda f}v)$ at $df_x=\xi$). Suppose $p(x,\xi)$ is a Hermitian matrix satisfying $p(x,\xi)\ge c|\xi|^2I$ for some $c>0$. Assume its nonnegative selfadjoint realization has a complete orthonormal basis of smooth eigensections and a smooth heat kernel $K_t(y,z):E_z\to E_y$ relative to Riemannian volume. No scalar-principal-symbol hypothesis is imposed. In normal coordinates and smooth unitary frames based at $x$, set

$$k_x(w)=(2\pi)^{-n}\int_{\mathbb R^n}e^{iw\cdot\xi}e^{-p(x,\xi)}\,d\xi.$$

Then $k_x$ is Schwartz, meaning it is smooth and $p_{\alpha,\beta}(k_x)=\sup_{w\in\mathbb R^n}\|w^\alpha\partial_w^\beta k_x(w)\|<\infty$ for every pair of multi-indices $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb N_0^n$, $\int k_x(w)\,dw=I$, and, locally uniformly for bounded $a,b\in T_xM$,

$$t^{n/2}K_t(\exp_x(\sqrt t\,a),\exp_x(\sqrt t\,b))\longrightarrow k_x(a-b).$$

For every integer $L>n$ there is $C_L$ such that

$$\|K_t(y,z)\|\le C_Lt^{-n/2}(1+d(y,z)/\sqrt t)^{-L}\qquad(0<t\le1).$$

In dimension zero the corresponding assertion is the finite-dimensional limit $K_t(x,x)\to I$ and zero kernel between distinct points.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim: At a simple fixed point $x$, the inverse function theorem makes $x$ isolated in $M^g$; since $M^g$ is closed in compact $M$, it is finite. Choose disjoint sufficiently small normal neighborhoods of these points. In normal coordinates the isometry satisfies $g^{-1}\exp_x(\sqrt t\,v)=\exp_x(\sqrt t\,dg_x^{-1}v)$. For the trace-integral identity, factor $U_ge^{-t\Delta}=(U_ge^{-t\Delta/2})e^{-t\Delta/2}$. Both factors have smooth kernels on compact $M$ and finite Hilbert–Schmidt norm. Expansion in an orthonormal basis and Cauchy–Schwarz make the integrated product absolutely summable, giving its trace as the integral of the composed diagonal kernel. The section-action convention in [F1] therefore identifies the trace integrand with $\sum_j(-1)^j\operatorname{tr}(\rho_g^j(g^{-1}y) K_t^j(g^{-1}y,y))$.

Use the positive-frequency convention $\sigma_1(d_j)(x,\xi)=\sum_{|\alpha|=1}a_{j,\alpha}(x)(i\xi)^\alpha$. Integration by parts gives $\sigma_1(d_j^*)=\sigma_1(d_j)^*$ in this convention. Put $B_j=\sigma_1(d_j)(x,\xi)$, with $B_{-1}=B_N=0$. The principal symbol on $E^j$ of $\Delta$ is $p_j=B_j^*B_j+B_{j-1}B_{j-1}^*$. If its quadratic form vanishes on $v$, then $B_jv=0$ and $B_{j-1}^*v=0$; exactness gives $v\in\operatorname{im}B_{j-1}$ and also orthogonality to that image, hence $v=0$. Compactness of the unit cotangent sphere bundle gives $p_j(x,\xi)\ge c|\xi|^2I$ uniformly. Thus [L1] applies to $\Delta$, using exactly the given spectral heat data. Its principal symbol may be matrix-valued.

Write $n=\dim M$ and $J_x$ for the normal-coordinate volume density. For $y=\exp_x(\sqrt t\,v)$ in the chosen neighborhood, [L1] and step 1.1 imply that $t^{n/2}J_x(\sqrt t\,v)\sum_j(-1)^j\operatorname{tr}(\rho_g^j(g^{-1}y) K_t^j(g^{-1}y,y))$ tends pointwise to $\sum_j(-1)^j\operatorname{tr}(\rho_g^j|_{E_x^j}\,k_x^j(dg_x^{-1}v-v))$. Simplicity makes $dg_x^{-1}-I$ invertible. Local distance comparison in the normal chart therefore gives $d(g^{-1}y,y)\ge c_x\sqrt t\,|v|$. Choose $L>n$; bounded density, unitary $\rho_g$ and [L1] bound the extended-by-zero rescaled density by $C(1+c_x|v|)^{-L}$, integrable on $T_xM$. Outside these neighborhoods compactness gives $d(g^{-1}y,y)\ge\delta>0$, so [L1] bounds the full complementary trace integral by $C t^{(L-n)/2}\to0$. By [F2], the heat-supertrace limit is consequently the sum of these tangent integrals. No uniform-integral-bound-to-convergence implication is used.

Since $dg_x$ is orthogonal, $|\det(dg_x^{-1}-I)|=|\det(I-dg_x)|$. The change of variables $w=(dg_x^{-1}-I)v$ therefore contributes $|\det_{\mathbb R}(I-dg_x)|^{-1}$. By [L1], the constant-coefficient tangent heat kernel has integral $I_{E_x^\bullet}$. Its graded fiber trace after composition with $\rho_g$ is $\sum_j(-1)^j\operatorname{tr}(\rho_g|_{E_x^j})$. For $n=0$, the tangent integral and determinant are both the empty-dimensional values $1$, so the same expression holds. Summing the finitely many contributions proves the stated limit.

Work in $\mathrm{ZF}+\mathrm{AC}$. Let $T=(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^r$, $r\ge0$, act continuously on a locally compact Hausdorff space $X$. All vector bundles below have finite complex rank and continuous $T$-linearizations. A **compact-support symbol triple** is $(A,B,s)$, where $A,B\to X$ are such bundles and $s:A\to B$ is an equivariant bundle map that is an isomorphism outside an invariant compact subset of $X$. Isomorphic triples have intertwining bundle isomorphisms. A homotopy of triples is such a triple over $X\times[0,1]$, with trivial action on $[0,1]$, whose noninvertibility set lies in $C\times[0,1]$ for some invariant compact $C\subset X$. A triple is elementary when $s$ is an isomorphism on all of $X$.

Define $K^0_{T,c}(X)$ to be the abelian group on isomorphism classes of these triples, subject to the relations that direct sum is addition, elementary triples are zero, and the two endpoints of a homotopy represent the same class. Define $K^1_{T,c}(X)=K^0_{T,c}(X\times\mathbb R)$, with trivial action on $\mathbb R$. Here $c$ means compact support. For any base $Y$, write $K_T^0(Y)$ for the Grothendieck ring of equivariant vector bundles on $Y$. On compact $Y$, the natural map $[W]\mapsto[W,0,0]$ identifies this with the triple presentation: $s$ can be homotoped to zero, and $(W,W,I)$ can be homotoped to $(W,W,0)$, giving precisely the direct-sum and inverse relations. On a point the bundle Grothendieck ring is the representation ring $R(T)$, whose multiplication is tensor product and whose element $[W]$ has character $g\mapsto\operatorname{tr}(g|W)$. Tensoring both bundles and the map of a triple with the pullback of a representation defines the $R(T)$-module structure on $K^q_{T,c}(X)$, $q=0,1$.

For a smooth compact $T$-manifold $M$, give $T^*M$ the cotangent action: $t$ sends $(x,\xi)$ to $(t\cdot x,\xi\circ(dt_x)^{-1})$. Let $A:C^\infty(M,E^+)\to C^\infty(M,E^-)$ be a first-order differential operator between smooth finite-rank equivariant complex bundles. The smooth bundle actions have fiber maps $\rho_t^\pm(x):E_x^\pm\to E_{t\cdot x}^\pm$, satisfying $\rho_e^\pm(x)=I$ and $\rho_{st}^\pm(x)=\rho_s^\pm(t\cdot x)\rho_t^\pm(x)$; on sections set $(U_t^\pm u)(x)=\rho_t^\pm(t^{-1}\cdot x)u(t^{-1}\cdot x)$. Require $AU_t^+=U_t^-A$. If $A=\sum_{|\alpha|\le1}a_\alpha(x)\partial_x^\alpha$ in local coordinates and frames, put $a(x,\xi)=\sum_{|\alpha|=1}a_\alpha(x)(i\xi)^\alpha$. The operator is elliptic when $a(x,\xi):E_x^+\to E_x^-$ is invertible for every real $\xi\ne0$. Its **compact symbol class** is

$$[\sigma(A)]=[\pi^*E^+,\pi^*E^-,a]\in K^0_{T,c}(T^*M),$$

where $\pi:T^*M\to M$ is the projection. The zero section is compact; the differential intertwining identity makes its symbol equivariant. Choose invariant smooth bundle metrics, a positive invariant smooth density, and invariant connections. Here $L^2(M,E)$ is the completion of smooth sections in the resulting squared-integral norm, and $H^1(M,E)$ is their completion in the norm $\|u\|_{H^1}^2=\|u\|_{L^2}^2+\|\nabla u\|_{L^2}^2$. A bounded realization $A:H^1(M,E^+)\to L^2(M,E^-)$ is **Fredholm** when $\ker A$ is finite dimensional, $\operatorname{ran}A$ is closed, and $\operatorname{coker}A:=L^2(M,E^-)/\operatorname{ran}A$ is finite dimensional. If this realization is Fredholm, its **analytic equivariant index** is $[\ker A]-[\ker A^*]\in R(T)$, where $A^*:L^2(M,E^-)\to H^1(M,E^+)$ is the bounded Hilbert-space adjoint for these norms; its kernel is the orthogonal complement of $\operatorname{ran}A$, hence represents the cokernel. These finite-dimensional kernels carry the induced $T$-representations. Fredholmness is a hypothesis here, not a consequence stipulated by the definition.

For a Hermitian equivariant complex vector bundle $W\to Y$, write $\pi_W:W\to Y$ for its projection. On $\pi_W^*\Lambda^\bullet W$ define $\varepsilon_w$ to be exterior multiplication by the tautological vector $w\in W_y$, and let $\varepsilon_w^*$ be its Hermitian adjoint. The **Koszul symbol** is $\kappa_W=(\varepsilon_w+\varepsilon_w^*)|_{\mathrm{ev}}$ from even to odd exterior powers. It satisfies $(\varepsilon_w+\varepsilon_w^*)^2=|w|^2I$, so it is invertible off the zero section. On a complex line with coordinate $z$, its even-to-odd map is multiplication by $z$; this fixes its Bott sign. If $Y$ is noncompact, this is a class with support proper over $Y$, not a compact-support class on $W$ by itself. Its zero-section restriction is the virtual bundle

$$\lambda_{-1}(W)=\sum_{j=0}^{\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb C}W}(-1)^j[\Lambda^jW]\in K_T^0(Y).$$

For a real equivariant normal bundle $\nu\to F$ supplied with an invariant inner product, identify $\nu^*$ with $\nu$. The doubled normal bundle $\nu\oplus\nu^*$ has complex structure $J(v,w)=(-w,v)$, so is identified with $\nu_{\mathbb C}=\nu\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb C$. The real inner product extends complex-bilinearly to a nondegenerate equivariant pairing on $\nu_{\mathbb C}$, hence gives a complex-linear equivariant isomorphism $\nu_{\mathbb C}\cong\nu_{\mathbb C}^*$. Its Koszul zero-section class $\lambda_{-1}(\nu_{\mathbb C})$ can therefore also be written $\lambda_{-1}(\nu_{\mathbb C}^*)$. This identification is asserted for a complexified real bundle, not for an arbitrary Hermitian complex bundle. For $g\in T$ fixing the base point $x\in F$, the character of this virtual fiber is

$$\operatorname{tr}\!\left(g\middle|\lambda_{-1}(\nu_{\mathbb C,x}^*)\right)=\det_{\mathbb C}(I-g|_{\nu_{\mathbb C,x}^*}).$$

This follows by expanding the exterior-power trace as the product of $1-\lambda$ over the complex eigenvalues $\lambda$. For orthogonal $g$, this determinant equals the real determinant $\det_{\mathbb R}(I-g|_{\nu_x})$ and is positive when $g$ has no fixed normal vector: nonreal eigenvalues occur in conjugate pairs, and a real eigenvalue different from $1$ is $-1$.

Assume AC. Let $T=(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^r$ act smoothly on compact smooth manifolds without boundary. The compact-symbol triple group has a homomorphism

$$a_{T,M}:K^0_{T,c}(T^*M)\longrightarrow R(T)$$

which sends the symbol of an equivariant elliptic operator to its analytic kernel-minus-adjoint-kernel index, and sends the folded symbol of a first-order elliptic complex to its alternating cohomology representation. It is $R(T)$-linear and respects equivariant diffeomorphisms and restriction of the acting group.

Let $f:Y\hookrightarrow M$ be a smooth equivariant embedding of compact manifolds, with real invariant metric normal bundle $N$. Extend a covector on $Y$ by zero on $N$ to obtain $j:T^*Y\hookrightarrow T^*M$. Its normal bundle is $\pi_Y^*(N\oplus N^*)$, with complex structure $J(v,\eta)=(-\eta^\sharp,v^\flat)$. Define $j_!$ by pulling a symbol to this complex normal, taking its graded product with exterior multiplication by $v+i\eta^\sharp$ plus its adjoint on $\Lambda^\bullet N_{\mathbb C}$, and extending from a tubular neighborhood. Then, for every $c\in K^0_{T,c}(T^*Y)$,

$$a_{T,M}(j_!c)=a_{T,Y}(c).$$

This includes arbitrary symbol classes and real normal bundles, without a Dirac-type or fixed-point-dimension restriction.

For the trivial group, embed $Y$ into $\mathbb R^N$ and form the same doubled-normal extension $j_!c\in K_c^0(T^*\mathbb R^N)$. This group is generated by the plane Bott product with plane map $z=x+i\xi$. Its integer coefficient is denoted $p_{Y,!}(c)$. One has

$$a_{\{1\},Y}(c)=p_{Y,!}(c).$$

In particular that integer is independent of the embedding. If $g\in T$ fixes $Y$ pointwise, its action splits a symbol into finitely many $g$-eigenbundle classes $c_\lambda$ on each compact disk representative, and

$$\chi_{a_{T,Y}(c)}(g)=\sum_\lambda\lambda\,p_{Y,!}(c_\lambda).$$

Every identity extends to localization at the virtual representations whose character at $g$ is nonzero, by division by that character. No assertion of an index distribution for transversally elliptic symbols is made.

Assume AC. Let $T=(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^r$ act smoothly on a compact smooth manifold $M$ without boundary. Fix $g\in T$, put $F=M^g$, and choose a $T$-invariant metric. Write $\nu=(TF)^\perp\subset TM|_F$, $p:T^*F\to F$, and $X=T^*M$. The inclusion $j:T^*F\to X$ extends a covector by zero on $\nu$. It is a proper embedding and $X^g=j(T^*F)$. Its real normal bundle is $p^*(\nu\oplus\nu^*)$, with complex structure $J(v,\eta)=(-\eta^\sharp,v^\flat)$, hence is the complex bundle $W=p^*\nu_{\mathbb C}$. Put

$$e=\lambda_{-1}(\nu_{\mathbb C}^*)\in K_T^0(F),\qquad S_g=\{s\in R(T):s(g)\ne0\}.$$

Here $s(g)$ is the character value of the virtual representation $s$; localization means tensoring an $R(T)$-module with $S_g^{-1}R(T)$. In both degrees $q=0,1$, restriction is an isomorphism

$$j^*:S_g^{-1}K^q_{T,c}(T^*M)\xrightarrow{\cong}S_g^{-1}K^q_{T,c}(T^*F).$$

The Koszul symbol on $W$, followed by extension from a tubular neighborhood, defines a homomorphism $j_!:K^q_{T,c}(T^*F)\to K^q_{T,c}(T^*M)$. Its self-intersection formula and localized reconstruction formula are

$$j^*j_!(b)=p^*e\,b,\qquad a=j_!\bigl((p^*e)^{-1}j^*a\bigr).$$

The inverse in the second formula exists as a module endomorphism after $S_g$-localization. These identities hold for every compact-support symbol class, including the class of every equivariant elliptic operator, with no Dirac-type or isolated-fixed-point restriction.

Let $E\to F$ be a finite-rank complex $T$-equivariant bundle. Since $g$ fixes $F$ pointwise, its induced bundle automorphism has eigenbundles $E_\zeta$. The $g$-character homomorphism is $\operatorname{tr}_g[E]=\sum_\zeta\zeta[E_\zeta]\in K^0(F)\otimes\mathbb C$, extended additively to virtual bundles and to fractions by division by $s(g)$. For the denominator it gives

$$\operatorname{tr}_g(e)=\prod_\zeta\left(\sum_{k=0}^{\operatorname{rank}E_\zeta}(-\zeta)^k[\Lambda^kE_\zeta]\right),\qquad E=\nu_{\mathbb C}^*.$$

Every eigenvalue $\zeta$ here differs from $1$. The rank of this ordinary $K$-class at $x\in F$ is $\det_{\mathbb C}(I-g|_{\nu_{\mathbb C,x}^*})=\det_{\mathbb R}(I-g|_{\nu_x})\ne0$. At an isolated fixed point this is exactly the real determinant. On a positive-dimensional component the whole virtual bundle, rather than just its rank, is required in the reconstruction formula.

Assume AC. Let $T=(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^r$, where $r\ge0$, act smoothly on a compact smooth manifold $F$ without boundary, possibly disconnected and nonorientable. Fix $h\in T$ whose action on $F$ is the identity. All vector bundles below have finite complex rank and continuous $T$-linearizations; use $T$-invariant Hermitian metrics. The induced $h$-action on each bundle then covers the identity and is unitary. Put $n=\dim F$ componentwise and let $\pi:T^*F\to F$ be the cotangent projection. For a compact space $Y$ of finite CW homotopy type, choose a homotopy equivalence $f:C\to Y$ from a finite CW complex and define the ordinary character on $Y$ by $\operatorname{ch}_Y(v)=(f^*)^{-1}\operatorname{ch}_C(f^*v)$. For a compact pair $(Y,Z)$ admitting a finite CW pair model, choose a homotopy equivalence of pairs $f:(C,D)\to(Y,Z)$ and define $\operatorname{ch}_{(Y,Z)}(v)=(f^*)^{-1}\operatorname{ch}_{(C,D)}(f^*v)$. The inverse $f^*$ here is the cohomology isomorphism; the inner pullback is in bundle K-theory. These definitions are independent of the models, as proved below. Compact smooth bases have such models; disk/sphere bundle pairs have finite pair models by pulling the bundle to a finite base model and attaching its disk fibers over the finitely many cells. Define $\operatorname{ch}_c$ on $T^*F$ using this relative character on a closed disk/sphere pair $(D_R(T^*F),S_R(T^*F))$ containing the symbol support in its interior, then its image in compact-support cohomology under excision. Radii are identified by radial deformation and extension, so this defines one class. Chern classes used below, and hence the Todd polynomials in them, are transported by the same inverse-cohomology-pullback convention. Follow all rational characters by $\mathbb Q\hookrightarrow\mathbb C$ when taking weighted sums.

For an equivariant vector bundle $W\to F$, define $(W_\lambda)_x=\ker(h|_{W_x}-\lambda I)$ for each eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $h$. These are $T$-equivariant subbundles: the compact closure of $\langle h\rangle$ acts trivially on $F$, and averaging over its characters gives continuous eigenprojections of locally constant rank. Compactness of $F$ makes the total eigenvalue list finite. For an absolute equivariant virtual bundle $V\in K_T^0(F)$, set

$$\operatorname{ch}_h(V)=\sum_\lambda\lambda\,\operatorname{ch}(V_\lambda)\in H^{\mathrm{even}}(F;\mathbb C),$$

where the sum is extended additively from actual bundles to virtual classes, and $\operatorname{ch}$ denotes the ordinary rational Chern character followed by the coefficient inclusion $\mathbb Q\hookrightarrow\mathbb C$. For a compact-support symbol class $a$ on $T^*F$, whose symbol bundles and map are $T$-equivariant, define its trace-weighted compact-support Chern character by

$$\operatorname{ch}_{h,c}(a)=\sum_{\lambda}\lambda\,\operatorname{ch}_c(a_\lambda)\in H_c^{\mathrm{even}}(T^*F;\mathbb C),$$

where $a_\lambda$ is its symbol class on the $\lambda$-eigenbundles of $h$. The sum is finite on each compact disk-bundle representative; it is extended linearly to virtual classes. $$\mathcal F(\partial^\alpha f)(\xi)=(2\pi i\xi)^\alpha\widehat f(\xi),\qquad \partial^\beta\widehat f=\mathcal F((-2\pi ix)^\beta f).$$

Assume countable choice. For every $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$ and every $x\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$f(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\widehat f(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\,d\xi.$$
The integral is absolutely convergent.
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every open cover of a smooth manifold admits a smooth partition of unity subordinate to it.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: Work in one precompact bundle chart and write $p(y,\xi)=\sum A^{ij}(y)\xi_i\xi_j$. The matrices need not commute. For a parameter derivative, the matrix exponential satisfies $\partial e^{-p}=-\int_0^1e^{-(1-s)p}(\partial p)e^{-sp}\,ds$, obtained by differentiating the matrix ODE defining the exponential. Iterating this identity and differentiating in $\xi$ expresses every derivative in $y,\xi$ as finitely many simplex integrals of products of polynomial derivatives of $p$ and exponential factors whose time lengths sum to one. Since $p\ge c'|\xi|^2I$ uniformly on the chart closure, the product norm is at most a polynomial in $|\xi|$ times $e^{-c'|\xi|^2}$. Thus $e^{-p(y,\cdot)}$ is a uniformly bounded smooth Schwartz family. By [F1] its inverse transform $k_y(w)$ has all uniformly bounded Schwartz seminorms, and $\int k_y(w)\,dw=e^{-p(y,0)}=I$. This uses Fourier inversion on Schwartz functions, not an exchange of an undamped double Fourier integral.

Let $\kappa_i$ be finitely many charts with smooth unitary frames, and let $\phi_i$ be a partition subordinate to compact subsets of those charts. Choose smooth cutoffs $\chi_i(y,z)$ supported where both points lie in chart $i$, equal to one near $y=z$ whenever $z\in\operatorname{supp}\phi_i$. Write volume as $w_i(z)\,d\kappa_i(z)$. Define $Z_t(y,z)$ in these frames by the finite sum of $\phi_i(z)\chi_i(y,z)w_i(z)^{-1}t^{-n/2}k_{i,z}((\kappa_i(y)-\kappa_i(z))/\sqrt t)$, interpreting each summand as a bundle map. In each summand the principal coefficients are frozen at the source $z$. Step 1.1, local equivalence of chart distance and $d$, and cutoff support give $\|Z_t(y,z)\|\le C_LH_{t,L}(y,z)$, where $H_{t,L}=t^{-n/2}(1+d(y,z)/\sqrt t)^{-L}$. Moreover $Z_tf\to f$ in $L^2$ for smooth $f$: put $\kappa_i(y)-\kappa_i(z)=\sqrt t\,v$, use the uniform integrable Schwartz bound, and use $\sum_i\phi_i=1$ and $\int k_{i,y}=I$. For $R_t=(\partial_t+P_y)Z_t$, the frozen principal part cancels $\partial_t$. The remaining principal term contains $A(y)-A(z)=O(d(y,z))$ and two derivatives of the frozen kernel; lower terms contain at most one derivative. The bound $d(y,z)t^{-1}H_{t,L+1}\le t^{-1/2}H_{t,L}$ therefore gives $\|R_t(y,z)\|\le C_Lt^{-1/2}H_{t,L}(y,z)$. Derivatives of cutoffs are supported away from the diagonal and obey the same bound by choosing additional Schwartz decay.

Fix $L>n$. Uniform volume bounds in the finite atlas give $\sup_y\int H_{t,L}(y,z)\,dz+\sup_z\int H_{t,L}(y,z)\,dy\le C_L$. Also $\int H_{a,L}(y,u)H_{b,L}(u,z)\,du\le C_LH_{a+b,L}(y,z)$ for $a,b>0$, $a+b\le1$. To check the second estimate, suppose $a\le b$ and put $r=d(y,z)$. If $r\le\sqrt b$, bound the second factor by $b^{-n/2}$ and integrate the first. If $r>\sqrt b$, split into $d(y,u)\ge r/2$ and its complement. On the first set, the first factor is bounded by $C a^{(L-n)/2}r^{-L}\le C b^{(L-n)/2}r^{-L}$; integrate the second. On the complement, $d(u,z)\ge r/2$, so bound the second factor by $C b^{(L-n)/2}r^{-L}$ and integrate the first. These bounds are comparable to $H_{a+b,L}(y,z)$; exchanging the factors treats $b\le a$.

Define Volterra convolution by $(A*B)_t(y,z)=\int_0^t\int_M A_{t-s}(y,u)B_s(u,z)\,du\,ds$. The residual bound and step 3.1 show $\|R*R\|\le C H_{t,L}$, since $\int_0^t((t-s)s)^{-1/2}\,ds=\pi$ (substitute $s=t\sin^2\theta$). Iterating this bounded time kernel gives $\|R^{*(2m)}_t\|\le C^{2m}t^{m-1}H_{t,L}/(m-1)!$ after enlarging $C$. Convolving once more with $R$ gives $\|R^{*(2m+1)}_t\|\le 2C^{2m+1}t^{m-1/2}H_{t,L}/(m-1)!$ for $m\ge1$, by bounding $s^{m-1}\le t^{m-1}$ in the time integral; $R$ itself has its original bound. Consequently $Q=\sum_{m\ge1}(-1)^mR^{*m}$ converges absolutely on every positive-time compact set, has $\|Q_t\|\le C t^{-1/2}H_{t,L}$ for $t\le1$, and satisfies $Q+R+R*Q=0$. Fubini and associativity hold because every displayed absolute convolution bound is finite. Hence $S=Z+Z*Q$ satisfies $\|S_t-Z_t\|\le C\sqrt t H_{t,L}$ and $S_tf\to f$ in $L^2$ for smooth $f$.

Extend kernels causally by zero for negative time. The initial limit of $Z$ gives $(\partial_t+P_y)Z=\delta_0I+R$ in distributions. Applying this identity to the absolutely convergent convolutions of step 4.1 yields $(\partial_t+P_y)S=\delta_0I+R+Q+R*Q=\delta_0I$. These distribution identities can equivalently be verified first on $\varepsilon<s<t-\varepsilon$, tested against a compactly supported smooth function of time and space, and then passed to the endpoints using the integrable bounds from step 4.1. Thus no differentiation of a singular convolution is assumed pointwise. For smooth initial $f$, let $\psi$ be a smooth eigensection of $P$ with eigenvalue $\lambda$. Formal symmetry and the distribution equation give $a'(t)+\lambda a(t)=0$ for $a(t)=\langle S_tf,\psi\rangle$, with $a(0)=\langle f,\psi\rangle$. Therefore $a(t)=e^{-t\lambda}\langle f,\psi\rangle$. The two-sided integral bounds in step 3.1 make $S_t$ bounded on $L^2$ (apply Cauchy–Schwarz with weight $\|S_t(y,z)\|$). Completeness of the given eigenbasis proves $S_t=e^{-tP}$ on $L^2$. The series and convolutions define continuous kernels for $t>0$: on time intervals away from the endpoints use uniform convergence, and bound the omitted endpoint intervals by the integrable convolution estimates. Equality as distributions with the smooth given $K_t$ therefore gives $S_t(y,z)=K_t(y,z)$ everywhere. In particular the bound for $S$ is the stated bound for $K$.

Fix $x$ and put $y=\exp_x(\sqrt t\,a)$, $z=\exp_x(\sqrt t\,b)$. In a chart, Taylor expansion gives $(\kappa_i(y)-\kappa_i(z))/\sqrt t\to d\kappa_i|_x(a-b)$, the frozen symbol tends to $p_i(x,\xi)$, and all frame maps, partition weights and density factors tend to their values at $x$. Linear change of cotangent variables in the absolutely convergent Fourier integral transforms each limiting chart expression into $\phi_i(x)k_x(a-b)$: the coordinate Jacobian cancels $w_i(x)$ because normal-coordinate volume density at $x$ is one. Summing gives $k_x(a-b)$. All convergences are uniform on bounded $a,b$ by step 1.1. By step 4.1, $t^{n/2}\|K_t-Z_t\|\le C\sqrt t$, so it has zero limit. This proves the rescaled limit and all assertions for $n>0$. If $M$ is empty the claims are vacuous; for $n=0$, compact $M$ is finite and differential operators act separately on its fibers, so ordinary matrix exponentiation gives exactly the asserted finite-dimensional limit.
